841.title: Ibn Arabi's heart
841.hook: Ibn Arabi wrote that his heart had become able to take every form, in his own Sufi sense (Tarjuman al-Ashwaq 11)
841.howItsDone: Ibn Arabi's writings are studied in Sufi circles and universities alike, and this poem from the Tarjuman al-Ashwaq is often read together with his own commentary on it.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the astrolabe: love, for Rumi, as an instrument you look through toward its source. Your line was a love you can look through. Today, one more Sufi voice, about a heart that keeps changing shape.

Water has no shape of its own. Pour it into a cup and it's cup-shaped; into a vase, vase-shaped; into a cupped hand, it fits the hand. Nobody calls the water unfaithful for that. A Muslim mystic named Ibn Arabi, writing in Arabic, said something like that about his own heart. In a book of love poems, he wrote that his heart had become able to take every form.
screen: `WATER HAS NO SHAPE.` → `IT FITS WHAT HOLDS IT.` → `A HEART ABLE TO TAKE EVERY FORM.`

segments.voice: The collection is called the Interpreter of Desires. Ibn Arabi writes, in paraphrase: my heart has become able to take every form. It is a pasture for gazelles, a cloister for monks, a temple for idols, the Kaaba of the pilgrim, the tablets of the Torah and the book of the Quran. Then: I follow the religion of love, wherever its camels turn. Around it is a love poem, full of longing for a beloved, ruined campsites and departing caravans, the old images of Arabic love poetry. Tradition says some readers objected that the poems were simply worldly love songs, and Ibn Arabi answered by writing a commentary on them, reading each image as a sign of divine knowledge. Readers hear the poem two ways. Some hear it saying every religion is the same. Others hear something narrower and stranger: a Muslim heart so turned toward God that it can recognize God's self-disclosure wherever it appears. This lesson doesn't choose between them. Either way, the image is a heart that doesn't harden into one shape against the world. It stays able to receive. Like water, it takes the form of what it meets, and stays water.
screen: `THE POEM: EVERY FORM.` · `A LOVE POEM AND ITS COMMENTARY.` · `TWO READINGS.` · `A HEART THAT STAYS OPEN.` · then, large: `IBN ARABI'S HEART.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a person or a place where you usually close up a little, a relative who talks politics, a neighborhood you avoid, a coworker who rubs you the wrong way, and notice what happens in your chest. Without agreeing or approving, picture your heart as water meeting that shape: it doesn't have to become them, it just doesn't have to turn to stone. If you pray, you can hold that person in your own tradition's words.

Your line: able to take every form. A heart can stay open without losing itself. Until tomorrow.

842.title: Mirabai's devotion
842.hook: Hindu bhakti poets like Mirabai loved Krishna with their whole lives
842.howItsDone: Hindus practice bhakti in many ways, among them temple worship, festivals, and singing devotional songs (bhajans and kirtan), and songs attributed to Mirabai are still sung in homes and temples.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Ibn Arabi, whose heart could take every form. Your line was able to take every form. That closes our Muslim and Sufi voices on love; today, Hindu voices begin.

A woman of a royal household walks out of the palace to sing in the temple with wandering holy men. She dances in front of an image of Krishna. Her in-laws are mortified: a woman of her rank should stay behind the walls, not sing in the street with strangers. She keeps singing anyway. Her name, as the stories give it, is Mirabai, and the songs said to be hers are still sung in homes and temples. Today's word is the thing she gave her whole life to.
screen: `A ROYAL WOMAN WALKS OUT.` → `SHE SINGS FOR KRISHNA.` → `HER NAME IS MIRABAI.`

segments.voice: Bhakti is Sanskrit, usually translated devotion: a loving, personal turning toward God. The Bhagavad Gita uses it, where Krishna speaks of those who worship him with bhakti, and it names whole movements of poet-saints who sang their love for God in everyday languages. Mirabai is one of them. Much of her story comes from legend, and the details vary. In the stories, she gives her heart to Krishna as a child and later calls him her true husband. Her new family tries to stop her devotion. Tradition says they even sent her poison, and she drank it as an offering, and it did her no harm. Her songs speak to Krishna directly, as someone near. One refrain, in paraphrase: mine is Giridhar Gopal, the cowherd who lifted the mountain, and no one else. They're plain and intimate, full of waiting, teasing, longing and joy, meant to be sung, not studied. For bhakti poets, devotion isn't a feeling saved for a holy day. It reorganizes everything: where you go, whom you sit with, what you sing while you work. Some Hindus practice bhakti through temple worship and festivals, others by chanting a name of God through the day. Mirabai's story shows what that love can cost, and, in the stories, she paid it singing.

Let the hum say thank you, or I miss you, or I'm glad you exist, and if it feels strange, hum softly anyway and notice where it vibrates in your chest. If you pray, a devotional song or name from your own tradition can take the place of the hum.

843.title: Radha and Krishna
843.hook: Jayadeva's Gita Govinda sings their love as divine love
843.howItsDone: Vaishnava Hindus worship Radha and Krishna together in temples and homes, and songs from the Gita Govinda and later devotional poets are sung in worship and danced in classical dance traditions.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was bhakti, and Mirabai singing for Krishna with her whole life. Your line was devotion. Today, a love story those songs return to.

Night in a forest by a river. Somewhere among the trees, someone is playing a flute. In the villages nearby, the cowherd women hear it, and in the Bhagavata Purana's telling, they drop what they're doing and go, out into the dark, toward the sound. The flute player is Krishna, the cowherd boy his devotees worship as God. Later poets give one of the women who love him a name and a story of her own: Radha. A Sanskrit poet named Jayadeva sang their love in a long poem called the Gita Govinda.
screen: `A FLUTE IN THE FOREST.` → `THE COWHERD WOMEN GO.` → `RADHA AND KRISHNA.`

segments.voice: In the Bhagavata Purana, Krishna's flute calls the cowherd women, the gopis, from their homes at night. Devotional readers hear it as God's call to the soul: a sound that makes everything else seem less urgent. The Gita Govinda tells a love story with a hurt in the middle. In spring, Krishna dances and plays with many gopis. Radha sees, and she is wounded. She withdraws into a bower in the forest and grieves, while Krishna misses her and longs for her. A friend of Radha's carries messages back and forth. At last Krishna comes to Radha, asks her pardon, and they are reunited. The poem dwells on their longing and their meeting in lush, frank detail, among flowers, bees and moonlight. Devotional readers don't take it as only a romance. For some Vaishnava devotees, Radha is the soul longing for God, or even the very power of God's own love. Her hurt, her waiting and her reunion become a map of devotion: the ache of separation, and the joy when God comes looking. The poem is sung in worship, not only recited as literature. Some traditions emphasize the longing; others the sweetness of the meeting. Both are there in the text.
screen: `THE FLUTE CALLS.` · `RADHA IS WOUNDED.` · `KRISHNA COMES BACK.` · `THEIR LOVE AS GOD'S LOVE.` · then, large: `RADHA AND KRISHNA.`

segments.voice: Put on a love song softly, any song from any time or place, or play one in your memory. Listen as if you were one of the gopis hearing the flute through the trees, not judging the song, just noticing what in you leans toward it, the longing and the sweetness, and then sit in the quiet after. If you pray, you can bring that longing into your own tradition's words.
Gita Govinda. Jayadeva's poem of Radha and Krishna's quarrel and reunion, read by devotees as the soul's longing for God answered. Today's word.
Your line: the flute. Some hear in it God's call to the soul. See you tomorrow.

844.title: Friendly to all
844.hook: Krishna: dear to me is one who hates no being, friendly and compassionate (Bhagavad Gita 12.13)
844.carry: a stranger at a bus stop
844.howItsDone: Hindus read and recite the Bhagavad Gita at home, in temples and in study groups, and its twelfth chapter, on devotion, is sometimes recited on its own.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the Gita Govinda, and the flute calling through the trees. Your line was the flute. Today, Krishna speaks again, about whom he holds dear.

A battlefield, two armies facing each other, and in the space between them a chariot. The warrior Arjuna has lost his nerve, and his charioteer, Krishna, is talking him through it. That conversation is the Bhagavad Gita. By its twelfth chapter, Arjuna has seen a vision of Krishna's cosmic form, and now he asks a quieter question: who knows yoga better, those who worship Krishna in a form, or those who worship the formless? Krishna's answer winds toward a portrait of a person. And the portrait starts with one who hates no being.
screen: `A CHARIOT BETWEEN ARMIES.` → `ARJUNA ASKS A QUIET QUESTION.` → `A PORTRAIT OF A PERSON.`

segments.voice: Krishna says, in paraphrase: the one who hates no being, who is friendly and compassionate, free from the sense of mine and free from ego, the same in pain and pleasure, and forgiving, that devotee is dear to me. Notice where it starts. Not with prayer or sacrifice: with hating no one. The word for friendly, in Sanskrit, is maitra. Not friends with all, as if everyone becomes your best friend. Friendly: a basic warmth toward every being, the default setting of the heart. Right beside it stands compassion, karuna, which feels for those who suffer. The same verse joins friendliness to letting go of possessiveness and ego. Some readers hear a link there: unfriendliness can grow out of mine. My seat, my way, my turn. When the grip on mine loosens, there's more room to be friendly. And then, dear to God. Earlier in the Gita, Krishna speaks of devotion as offering. Here he says who is dear to him: the person whose love has spilled outward into how they treat every creature. Devotion to God, in this verse, shows up as friendliness to everyone else. A stranger at a bus stop becomes part of the practice.

segments.voice: Picture a stranger you saw recently, someone in line, a driver, a person walking a dog, whose name and story you don't know. Let yourself be friendly toward them, not loving, not attached, just warm, the way you'd nod at a neighbor, and picture the nod you'd give if you passed them again tomorrow. If you pray, you can hold them in your own tradition's words.

845.title: Those who love
845.hook: Guru Gobind Singh: only those who love find the Lord (Tav-Prasad Savaiye)
845.carry: wealth can be held without love
845.howItsDone: Sikhs recite the Tav-Prasad Savaiye as part of Nitnem, the daily morning prayers, and the verses are also recited when the Khalsa initiation is given.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was maitra, friendly to all, in Krishna's portrait of the devotee. Your line was a stranger at a bus stop. Today, a Sikh voice on love.

Kings on elephants hung with gold. Armies in polished armor, horses dancing. Ascetics who've stood in cold rivers and gone without food. Pilgrims who've bathed at every holy place. A Sikh hymn walks you through a procession like that. Then, after all that spectacle, the poet stops and says, in effect: I tell you the truth, all of you, listen. Only those who love have found the Lord. The poet is Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru.
screen: `KINGS ON ELEPHANTS.` → `ASCETICS IN COLD RIVERS.` → `ONLY THOSE WHO LOVE.`

segments.voice: The verses are the Tav-Prasad Savaiye, by Guru Gobind Singh, part of Nitnem, the Sikh daily prayers said in the morning. They look at power, wealth and hard religious effort, one after another. Then comes the line the whole hymn leans on. In the original, in the old Braj language written in Gurmukhi, it begins sach kahon, I speak the truth. Then, in paraphrase: listen, everyone, only those who have loved have found the Lord. Jin prem kio, those who loved, tin hi prabh paio, they alone found God. The word for love there is prem. Notice what the line doesn't say. It doesn't call kings and ascetics bad, or mock pilgrimage. It says none of those, by itself, is the thing. Wealth can be held without love. Even fasting and cold baths can be done without love. The measure is not what you did, but whether you loved. And this love isn't soft. Guru Gobind Singh is remembered as a warrior-saint, who founded the Khalsa and stood against tyranny: a leader who knew armies firsthand, telling everyone that armies aren't what finds God. In Sikh teaching, love is the way to God, and it shows in remembering God's name, honest work and sharing with others.
screen: `THE HYMN AND ITS PARADE.` · `SACH KAHON: THE TURN.` · `WHAT THE LINE DOESN'T SAY.` · `LOVE THAT ISN'T SOFT.` · then, large: `THOSE WHO LOVE.`

segments.voice: Choose one thing to love with your whole heart, a person, the breath, the light in the room, the simple fact of being alive, and give it everything until the bell. When your mind drifts to plans or worries, the parade going by, come back to the one thing; loving here means returning. If you pray, you can bring a name of God from your own tradition into this.

Your line: wealth can be held without love. The Guru's measure is whether you loved. Day eight hundred forty-five.

846.title: As a mother
846.hook: as a mother protects her only child, so cultivate boundless love for all beings (Sutta Nipata 1.8)
846.howItsDone: Theravada Buddhists chant the Metta Sutta at home and in monasteries, and some Buddhists practice metta meditation, wishing well first to themselves or loved ones and then to all beings.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was prem: only those who love have found the Lord, in Guru Gobind Singh's hymn. Your line was wealth can be held without love. Today, a Buddhist voice.

A toddler wobbles toward the edge of a pool. Across the yard, a mother is already moving, before she's even decided to. Nothing else matters for that second: no meeting, no phone, no pride. There is one child, and she would put herself between that child and any harm. A short Buddhist text takes that instant, a fierce, protective love, and asks something startling. What if that love had no edges?
screen: `A TODDLER NEAR THE POOL.` → `A MOTHER ALREADY MOVING.` → `WHAT IF IT HAD NO EDGES?`

segments.voice: In the Metta Sutta, the discourse on loving-kindness, the Buddha says, in paraphrase: just as a mother would protect her only child with her own life, so one should cultivate a boundless heart toward all beings. Before that image comes a wish: may all beings be happy and at ease. Then the sutta spells out who all means. Weak or strong, long or short, large or small, seen or unseen, near or far, born or yet to be born. Nobody is left out by size or distance, or even by not being born yet. The sutta asks this love to spread above, below and all around, without obstruction, hatred or enmity. A mother's love is narrow: one child. The sutta keeps its intensity and takes away the walls. That's the turn. And it's for all times: standing, walking, sitting or lying down, as long as one is awake. Loving-kindness here isn't a mood for a quiet room; it goes wherever the body goes. The commentaries tell that the Buddha taught it to monks who were frightened in a forest. In Theravada communities the sutta is still chanted, at home and in monasteries.
screen: `THE IMAGE: A MOTHER'S LOVE.` · `MAY ALL BEINGS BE HAPPY.` · `BOUNDLESS: NO WALLS.` · `AT ALL TIMES.` · then, large: `AS A MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you'd protect without thinking, a child, a parent, a friend, a pet, and let that warmth come clearly. Keeping it, let the sutta's wish move outward, may all beings be happy and at ease: to people on your street, then people near and far you don't know, then every creature, seen and unseen. If the warmth thins, return to the one you'd protect and start again.
Metta. Loving-kindness, cultivated the way a mother would protect her only child, then stretched boundless toward all beings. Today's word.
Your line: boundless. A mother's fierce love, with the walls taken away. Until tomorrow, then.

847.title: Boundless compassion
847.hook: the second of the four boundless states in Buddhism
847.howItsDone: In Buddhist practice, compassion (karuna) is one of the four boundless states; Buddhaghosa's manual advises beginning by wishing one suffering person free of pain, then widening the wish step by step to all beings.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was metta: love like a mother's for her only child, with no edges. Your line was boundless. Today ends the week, and that love gets a second face.

An ambulance goes by with its siren on. Traffic pulls over. For a few seconds, a whole street of strangers knows that someone ahead is having one of the worst days of their life. Some drivers say a quiet word for whoever it is. Some just feel a tug in the chest, and then the light turns green. That tug has a name in Buddhism. Yesterday's love wished beings well; today's turns toward the ones who are hurting. It's the second of four states Buddhists call boundless.
screen: `A SIREN GOES BY.` → `A TUG IN THE CHEST.` → `THE SECOND BOUNDLESS STATE.`

segments.voice: Buddhist texts name four qualities a person can grow until they reach every being: loving-kindness, compassion, gladness for others, and equanimity. In the suttas, a meditator fills the world with each one in turn, one direction after another, until the whole world is covered. Karuna, compassion, is the second. It's the wish for someone to be free of their suffering. Not fixing them, not solving them: wishing, with the whole heart, that the pain would lift. Buddhaghosa, a Buddhist teacher, says in his manual the Path of Purification that compassion has a far enemy and a near one. The far enemy is plain: cruelty. The near enemy is sneakier, a sorrow that looks like compassion but sinks into its own grief, until the feeling is mostly about the one who feels it. Compassion stays turned toward the other person. Where to start? Not with everyone. Buddhaghosa says begin with one person you've seen in real misfortune, and let the wish grow: to someone dear, to someone you barely notice, and at last to someone you find hard. Boundless doesn't start boundless. It starts with one face.
screen: `FOUR STATES WITH NO EDGES.` · `THE WISH FOR SUFFERING TO LIFT.` · `A FAR ENEMY AND A NEAR ONE.` · `START WITH ONE FACE.` · then, large: `KARUNA.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who is suffering right now, someone sick, someone grieving, someone you saw on the street, and keep their face before you. Breathing in, notice their trouble without adding to it; breathing out, wish them free of it, in words as simple as may this lift, and if the feeling turns into your own heaviness, come back to their face. If you pray, you can hold them in a prayer from your own tradition.
Karuna. Compassion: the wish for one who suffers to be free of it, the second of the four boundless states. Today's word.
Your line: compassion. That ends a week of love in many voices: Ibn Arabi, Mirabai, Radha, the Gita, the Sikh hymn, the Metta Sutta, and now karuna. A week well walked.
